Give three models the same two hundred points, and each one draws a different border. Logistic regression draws a straight line. A decision tree cuts in steps. Nearest neighbors bends with the data. On points they haven't seen, they score eighty-two, eighty-nine and ninety-three percent. The model round asks how each one draws its border, and when you'd pick it. Of the fifteen questions here, eleven get a model fitted on screen, and four get a sentence each at the end. Start with the straight line.

Question one. What is logistic regression, and how does it output probabilities? It adds up the features into a score, the log odds, then passes that score through the sigmoid, which squeezes any number into the range zero to one. Here are five hundred sixty-nine tumors, and one feature: the mean radius of their cells. The score is minus fifteen point two five, plus one point oh three for each unit of radius. At a radius of fifteen, the score is point two six, and the sigmoid turns it into a probability of fifty-six percent. Each extra unit multiplies the odds of malignancy by two point eight. Question two. Why not linear regression for a binary target? Fit a straight line to the same zeros and ones, and it leaves the range: below zero for sixty tumors, above one for thirty-five. At a radius of twenty-eight, it predicts one point seven six, which no probability can be. Logistic regression stays inside, and it's fitted by maximum likelihood. Next, the model that cuts in steps.
